newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan prepares charges against Bhutto, husband.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan prepares charges against Bhutto, husband.

text.p: Pakistan's caretaker government said on Sunday it was preparing legal charges against ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto and her husband as she asked a court to free him from "illegal" detention.

Interim Prime Minister Meraj Khalid, asked if the government was preparing charges against Bhutto, told reporters: "Yes, yes." Asked if they would include criminal charges, he said: "All kinds of charges."
President Farooq Leghari sacked Bhutto and dissolved parliament last Tuesday, citing corruption, violence in Karachi and misrule he said had virtually paralysed the government.
He installed Khalid as head of an interim government to supervise elections set for February 3.

The caretaker prime minister was asked if the charges against Bhutto would include the violation of human rights in Karachi, riven by ethnic and sectarian violence. "Maybe, maybe, yes. Why not?" he said.

Khalid said the government was preparing charges against Bhutto's husband Asif Ali Zardari, who served as investment minister in his wife's cabinet and has been detained without charge since she was dismissed.
"In a very short while, these charges will be out and everyone will come to know why we detained or arrested him," Khalid said earlier at his maiden news conference.
Bhutto struck back on Sunday, filing a petition in Lahore High Court claiming Zardari was illegally detained, the official APP news agency said.
Zardari was picked up by soldiers in Lahore last Tuesday and later transferred to an official resthouse near Islamabad where he has been held under a law for the maintenance of public order.
Bhutto asked the court to order federal and local officials to release him, APP said.

But Khalid said Bhutto's husband was legally detained. "The law permits us, empowers us to detain him, and meanwhile we are framing those charges," he said, adding that the charges would be disclosed this week.
Bhutto's dismissal promises to lead to a string of court cases. She has vowed to challenge her ouster in the courts.
Asked if he believed the courts would uphold the president's order removing Bhutto from power, Khalid said: "I am here because I believe it was legal and regular."
Bhutto is no stranger to the courts.
In 1990, she was dismissed by then president Ghulam Ishaq Khan after 20 months in power and indicted on eight counts of abuse of power. She was later cleared of the charges.
In 1994 Zardari was cleared of the last of 13 similar charges brought against him after the first Bhutto government.

Bhutto, who was confined to the prime minister's official residence for 36 hours last week before curbs on her movement were lifted, has voiced fears that charges might be "fabricated" against Zardari.
She has denied that she or her husband, the focus of corruption allegations during her three years in office, were responsible for any wrongdoing.
Zardari has also been accused of conspiring to murder Bhutto's brother Murtaza, killed by police in Karachi on September 20. Zardari has denied the accusation.
A senior police officer accused of conspiring to murder Murtaza was arrested in Karachi on Sunday, police said.
